peoples.name: Yoruba
peoples.blurb: One of Africa's largest peoples, heirs to the sacred city of Ile-Ife, the Oyo Empire and one of the world's richest artistic and spiritual traditions.
sections: Overview

The Yoruba are one of the largest ethnic groups in Africa. Most live in south-western Nigeria, in states such as Oyo, Ogun, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti, Lagos and Kwara, with large communities in the Republic of Benin and Togo. Millions more of Yoruba descent live in Brazil, Cuba, Trinidad and the United States, where enslaved Yoruba people carried their language, music and religion across the Atlantic.

Historically the Yoruba were never a single kingdom. They were a family of city-states that shared a language, a creation story and a sacred centre at Ile-Ife. Each town had its own king (oba), palace, markets and festivals. This urban way of life is ancient: by the time Europeans arrived, Yoruba country was one of the most urbanised regions in Africa, with towns of tens of thousands of people.
Origins at Ile-Ife

In Yoruba tradition the world itself began at Ile-Ife. The supreme god Olódùmarè sent the orisha Obàtálá (in other versions Odùduwà) down a chain from the sky with a calabash of earth and a five-toed hen. The earth was poured onto the primeval waters, the hen scratched it out into dry land, and Ife became 'the place where the earth spread'.

Odùduwà is remembered as the first ruler of Ife and the ancestor of the Yoruba kings. His sons and grandsons are said to have left Ife to found the other kingdoms, including Oyo, Benin (through Oranmiyan), Ketu, Owu, Sabe and Popo. Because of this, almost every Yoruba crowned king traces his right to rule back to Ife, and the Ooni of Ife holds special spiritual seniority.

Archaeology shows that Ife was a major city by about 1000 CE. Between roughly the 12th and 15th centuries its artists created the famous Ife heads in copper alloy and terracotta: calm, naturalistic portraits so refined that early European visitors refused to believe Africans had made them. Ife was also a centre for glass bead making, one of the earliest in sub-Saharan Africa.
The Oyo Empire

From the 1600s the kingdom of Oyo, in the open savanna to the north, rose to become the most powerful Yoruba state. Its strength came from cavalry: horses bred and bought from the north gave Oyo armies speed that forest kingdoms could not match. At its height in the 18th century Oyo collected tribute from Dahomey and controlled trade routes reaching the coast at Porto-Novo and Badagry.

Oyo had a remarkable system of checks and balances. The king, the Aláàfin, ruled with a council of seven nobles called the Oyo Mesi, led by the Basorun. If the council lost confidence in a king, it could present him with an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, a signal that he must take his own life. A secret society, the Ogboni, balanced the power of the Oyo Mesi, and the army was led by a commander, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, who was expected never to retreat.

In the late 18th and early 19th centuries Oyo was torn by internal struggles, the revolt of its general Afonja at Ilorin and the spread of the Sokoto jihad from the north. Old Oyo was abandoned around 1835 and a new capital was built further south. The 19th century then saw long wars between Yoruba states such as Ibadan, Ijebu, Egba and the Ekiti confederacy, which ended with a British-brokered peace in 1886.
Society and government

Yoruba towns were organised around the palace (àáfin) and the market, which traditionally sat in front of the palace. Each town was divided into quarters headed by chiefs, and each quarter into compounds (agbo ilé) where extended families lived together around shared courtyards.

Power was rarely held by one person alone. Kings were sacred, often veiled with beaded crowns so their faces could not be seen, but they ruled through councils of chiefs, and powerful women held titles too. The Ìyálóde, the chief of the women, represented women's interests and the market traders, who were overwhelmingly women. Age, title and achievement mattered as much as birth.

Respect is central to Yoruba life. Younger people prostrate or kneel to greet elders, and the language itself has respectful pronouns for addressing seniors. The ideal person is described as having ìwà pẹ̀lẹ́, gentle good character, which is considered more beautiful than physical beauty.
Religion and the orisha

Traditional Yoruba religion recognises a supreme creator, Olódùmarè, and many orisha, divine forces who govern parts of nature and human life. Among the best known are Ọ̀ṣun, goddess of rivers, love and fertility; Ṣàngó, god of thunder and a deified king of Oyo; Ògún, god of iron, war and technology, to whom drivers and blacksmiths still pay respect; Yemọja, mother of waters; Èṣù, the messenger and keeper of crossroads; and Ọbàtálá, the pure white creator of human bodies.

Ifá divination is one of the great intellectual systems of Africa. A babaláwo (father of secrets) casts palm nuts or a divining chain to select one of 256 odù, each linked to hundreds of verses of poetry, stories and advice memorised over many years of training. UNESCO recognised the Ifá divination system as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005.

Today most Yoruba are Christian or Muslim, often in roughly equal numbers within the same family, yet orisha festivals remain important cultural events. The Ọ̀ṣun-Ọ̀ṣogbo Sacred Grove, a forest shrine on the Osun river, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and hosts a major festival every August.
Arts and crafts

Yoruba art is famous worldwide. Beyond the classical Ife heads, carvers created beaded crowns, palace doors, Ifá divination trays and twin figures called ère ìbejì. The Yoruba have one of the highest rates of twin births in the world, and when a twin died, a small carved figure was made and cared for as if it were the living child.

Adire is indigo-dyed cloth patterned by tying, stitching or painting starch onto the fabric before dyeing, a craft centred in Abeokuta. Aso-oke, a heavy hand-woven cloth, is worn for weddings and chieftaincy ceremonies. Gelede masks honour the power of mothers and elderly women, and Egúngún masquerades, covered in layers of rich cloth, represent ancestors who return to bless the living.
Music and the talking drum

The dùndún, the hourglass-shaped talking drum, can imitate the rising and falling tones of the Yoruba language, so a skilled drummer can literally speak praise names, proverbs and messages. Drum ensembles accompany festivals, kings and masquerades.

In the 20th century Yoruba musicians created juju music (King Sunny Adé, Ebenezer Obey), fuji (Ayinla Kollington, K1 De Ultimate) and contributed to Afrobeat through Fela Anikulapo Kuti, whose family came from Abeokuta. Today's Afrobeats stars such as Wizkid, Davido and Burna Boy often sing partly in Yoruba, carrying the language to global audiences.
Festivals and ceremonies

Naming ceremonies (ìsọmọlórúkọ) take place on the seventh day after a girl is born and the ninth day after a boy, traditionally the eighth for twins. The baby is introduced to symbolic items such as honey for sweetness, salt for flavour in life, kola nut, bitter kola for long life and water, and receives several names, each carrying meaning, such as Olúwaṣeun (God has done it) or Ayọ̀délé (joy has come home).

Major festivals include the Ọ̀ṣun-Ọ̀ṣogbo festival, the Olójó festival of Ife celebrating Ògún, Egúngún festivals honouring ancestors, the Eyo festival of Lagos with its white-robed masqueraders, and Ojude Oba in Ijebu-Ode, a spectacular parade of horsemen and age groups paying homage to the Awujale.
Food

Yoruba cuisine is rich and spicy. Àmàlà, a dark swallow made from yam flour, is eaten with ewédú (jute leaf soup) and gbẹ̀gìrì (bean soup), a famous combination in Ibadan. Pounded yam (iyán) is served with ẹ̀gúsí (melon seed) soup or èfọ́ rírò, a rich vegetable stew. Other favourites include mọ́in mọ́in (steamed bean pudding), àkàrà (bean fritters), ọ̀fadà rice with spicy pepper sauce, and the jollof rice that West Africans love to argue about.
Language and proverbs

Yoruba belongs to the Volta-Niger branch of the Niger-Congo family. It is tonal, with high, middle and low tones marked by accents: ọkọ́ means hoe, ọkọ̀ means vehicle and ọkọ means husband. Written Yoruba uses dots under letters such as ẹ, ọ and ṣ. The first Yoruba Bible translation was led in the 19th century by Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a formerly enslaved Yoruba boy who became the first African Anglican bishop.

Proverbs (òwe) are called the horses of speech: when words get lost, proverbs find them. Examples:
• 'Àgbà kì í wà lọ́jà, kí orí ọmọ tuntun wọ́.' An elder does not stand in the market while a baby's head is twisted (elders must guide the young).
• 'Ìkòkò tí yóò jẹ ata, ìdí rẹ̀ á gbóná.' The pot that will eat pepper must have its bottom burnt (success requires suffering).
Colonial era and today

Lagos was annexed by Britain in 1861, and the rest of Yoruba country came under British rule by the 1890s as part of the Colony and Protectorate of Southern Nigeria, later Nigeria (1914). Yoruba lawyers, journalists and politicians played leading roles in the nationalist movement; Chief Obafemi Awolowo founded the Action Group and introduced free primary education in the Western Region in 1955, one of the first such programmes in Africa.

Today Yoruba people are prominent in every field. Wole Soyinka became Africa's first Nobel laureate in Literature in 1986. Lagos, a Yoruba city at heart, is one of the largest and fastest-growing cities on earth and the engine of Nigeria's music, film (Nollywood) and technology industries.
Did you know?

• The Yoruba creation story says humans were shaped by Ọbàtálá from clay; people born with differences were once regarded as specially touched by him.
• Ilé-Ifẹ̀'s 'Ori Olokun' head and the 'Obalufon' mask are considered among the greatest metal sculptures ever made.
• Many Brazilian and Cuban words, songs and dishes come from Yoruba, and the religions Candomblé and Santería grew from orisha worship.

peoples.name: Igbo
peoples.blurb: A people of enterprise, learning and village democracy, creators of the 1,000-year-old Igbo-Ukwu bronzes and of some of Africa's greatest writers.
sections: Overview

The Igbo live mainly in south-eastern Nigeria, in Anambra, Enugu, Imo, Abia and Ebonyi states and parts of Delta and Rivers. They are one of Nigeria's three largest ethnic groups and are known across Africa for enterprise, trade, education and a strong attachment to their home villages, even when living far away.

Traditionally the Igbo did not have one great king. Most communities governed themselves through village assemblies, councils of elders, age grades and title societies, a system often described as a democracy of the village. A famous saying sums it up: 'Igbo enwe eze', the Igbo have no king.
Origins and early history

The Igbo heartland, east of the Niger River, has been inhabited for thousands of years. Pottery at Afikpo is among the oldest in West Africa, and iron smelting sites at Lejja and Opi near Nsukka are very old indeed, with some researchers arguing for dates in the first millennium BCE.

Igbo traditions of origin vary. Some communities say their ancestors came from the area around Nri and Aguleri in the Anambra valley; others hold that the Igbo have always lived where they are. Many share stories of Eri, a sky-descended founder who settled near the Anambra river and whose descendants founded Nri and Aguleri.
Igbo-Ukwu: bronzes of a thousand years

In 1938 a man digging a cistern in the town of Igbo-Ukwu found bronze objects. Excavations by the archaeologist Thurstan Shaw in 1959 and 1964 uncovered a shrine store, a burial chamber of an important person and a pit of ritual objects, dated to around the 9th and 10th centuries CE.

The Igbo-Ukwu bronzes are astonishing: vessels, shells, pendants and staffs decorated with tiny insects, snakes, beads and filigree, made by the lost-wax method with a skill unmatched anywhere in the world at that time. The site also held more than 100,000 glass and stone beads, some of which came from as far away as Egypt and India, showing that the Igbo world was linked to long-distance trade networks a thousand years ago.
The Kingdom of Nri

Nri was a unique state. From around the 10th century until the early 20th, the Eze Nri was a priest-king whose power was spiritual rather than military. Nri priests, marked by facial scars called ichi, travelled through Igboland to cleanse abominations, settle disputes, install titled men and bless farming. They declared certain acts nso, taboo, and could lift curses.

Nri promoted peace: its ritual agents could pass safely through warring towns, and Nri was associated with the abolition of human sacrifice and the protection of people seeking refuge. Nri influence declined in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the last Eze Nri of the old order, Obalike, died in 1936.
Society and government

An Igbo village was usually made up of several kindreds (umunna), descendants of a common ancestor. Decisions were made in open assemblies where any adult man could speak, and wisdom, wealth and eloquence won influence. Women had their own organisations, such as the umuada (daughters of the lineage) and the women's market and village councils, which could impose fines and even 'sit on' a man who broke the rules.

Age grades, groups of people born within a few years of each other, did public work such as clearing roads, building and policing. Title societies such as Ozo and Ọ̀zọ̀ gave status to men who had proved themselves through wealth and good character. The Igbo prize individual achievement: a person can rise through hard work, and success is celebrated.
Religion and beliefs

Traditional Igbo religion recognises Chukwu (also Chineke), the great creator, and many spirits and deities (alusi). Ala (or Ani), the earth goddess, is the most important: she is the guardian of morality, fertility and the dead, and offences against her are called nso ala. Amadioha is the god of thunder and justice, and Ikenga is a personal shrine representing a man's right hand, strength and achievement.

Each person is believed to have a chi, a personal spirit or guardian that shapes destiny. A well-known proverb says: 'Onye kwe, chi ya ekwe', when a person agrees, their chi agrees too. Ancestors remain part of the family and are honoured with libations and kola nut.

Today most Igbo are Christian, with large Catholic and Anglican communities and many Pentecostal churches, but cultural practices such as kola nut rituals and masquerades continue.
Arts and masquerades

Mbari houses, built in honour of Ala, were filled with painted clay sculptures of deities, people and scenes from daily life, created by artists over many months and then left to return to the earth. Uli is a graceful art of drawing on the body and on walls with dark plant dyes, practised mainly by women; its flowing lines inspired modern Nigerian artists of the Nsukka school such as Uche Okeke and Obiora Udechukwu.

Masquerades (mmanwu) are spirits of the ancestors who appear at festivals and funerals. Some are beautiful maidens (Agbogho Mmuo), others are fierce and dangerous; Ijele, a towering masquerade more than four metres high, is considered the king of masks and was recognised by UNESCO in 2009.
Festivals and the kola nut

The New Yam Festival (Iri Ji) marks the end of the farming season, usually in August. Yam is the king of crops in Igboland, and no one eats the new harvest until the eldest man or the traditional ruler has offered it to the ancestors and eaten the first yam. The festival brings dancing, masquerades, wrestling and feasting.

The kola nut (oji) is the symbol of hospitality and welcome. When a guest arrives, kola is presented, blessed, broken and shared. The number of lobes matters: three lobes is a sign of a brave or noble person, while a kola with only two lobes is not used in ritual. 'He who brings kola brings life,' goes the saying.
Food

Igbo cooking is famous across Nigeria. Popular dishes include ofe onugbu (bitterleaf soup), ofe oha, ofe nsala (white pepper soup), egusi soup and okra soup, eaten with swallows such as pounded yam, garri or fufu. Abacha (African salad) is made from shredded cassava with palm oil and ugba (fermented oil bean seeds). Nkwobi is a spicy cow-foot delicacy, and ugba and okpa (a steamed bambara-nut pudding) are favourite snacks.
Language and proverbs

Igbo is a tonal Niger-Congo language with many dialects; Standard Igbo, used in schools and media, is based largely on the speech of Owerri and Umuahia. In Chinua Achebe's words, 'proverbs are the palm oil with which words are eaten'.

• 'Egbe bere, ugo bere.' Let the kite perch and let the eagle perch (live and let live).
• 'Onye wetara oji, wetara ndụ.' He who brings kola brings life.
• 'Ihe onye metara, ọ ga-eburu.' Whatever a person does, they will carry.
Colonial era, war and today

British forces destroyed the Arochukwu oracle, Ibini Ukpabi, in the Anglo-Aro War of 1901 to 1902, and Igboland was brought under colonial rule. The British tried 'indirect rule' through appointed warrant chiefs, which clashed with Igbo democratic traditions and led to the Women's War of 1929 in Aba, when tens of thousands of women protested against taxation and abusive chiefs.

After independence, political crisis and massacres of Igbo in northern Nigeria led to the declaration of the Republic of Biafra in 1967 and a civil war that lasted until January 1970. More than a million people died, many from famine. After the war the Igbo rebuilt with remarkable speed.

Today Igbo traders run huge markets such as Onitsha Main Market and Alaba International in Lagos. The apprenticeship system, Igba Boi, in which young people serve a master trader and are then set up in business, has been praised by economists as one of the world's largest business incubators. Writers Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart, 1958) and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie have brought Igbo life to readers everywhere.
Did you know?

• Things Fall Apart has been translated into more than 50 languages and sold over 20 million copies.
• Nsibidi is an ancient system of symbols used in parts of south-eastern Nigeria, including by Igbo and Ejagham peoples, one of Africa's indigenous writing systems.
• The Igbo calendar has a four-day week: Eke, Orie, Afọ and Nkwọ, and markets are named after the day they are held.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Hausa
peoples.blurb: Builders of the walled city-states of Kano, Katsina and Zazzau, whose language became the great trade language of West Africa.
peoples.population: About 80 million first and second-language speakers
sections: Overview

The Hausa are the largest ethnic group in West Africa. They live mainly in northern Nigeria and southern Niger, with communities in Ghana, Cameroon, Chad, Sudan and along the old trade and pilgrimage routes across the Sahel. Hausa is spoken as a first or second language by tens of millions of people, making it one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa.

The Hausa are known for city life, trade, crafts and scholarship. For centuries their cities were among the most important markets of the trans-Saharan trade, linking the forests of the south with North Africa and the Mediterranean.
The Bayajidda legend

Hausa tradition tells of Bayajidda, a prince from the east (often said to be from Baghdad) who came to the town of Daura. The people could not draw water from the town well because a great snake, Sarki, lived in it. Bayajidda killed the snake, and the grateful queen, Magajiya Daurama, married him.

Their descendants founded the seven 'true' Hausa states, the Hausa Bakwai: Daura, Kano, Katsina, Zazzau (Zaria), Gobir, Rano and Biram. Seven other states with mixed populations, such as Kebbi, Nupe, Gwari, Yauri, Kwararafa (Jukun), Ilorin and Zamfara, were called the Banza Bakwai, the 'bastard' or illegitimate seven. Historians see the legend as a memory of new dynasties arriving and joining older local communities.
The city-states

From around the 11th century Hausa towns grew into walled city-states, each ruled by a sarki (king) from a palace at the centre. Kano, which grew around the iron-rich Dala hill, became the largest. Its huge earth walls, begun in the 11th and 12th centuries and later extended to around 14 to 20 kilometres in circumference, enclosed farmland as well as houses, so the city could survive a siege.

Katsina was a leading centre of trade and scholarship; Gobir was a warrior state guarding the north; Zazzau traded in enslaved people and kola from the south. The states often fought one another but were bound together by language, trade and, increasingly, Islam, which spread through merchants and scholars from Mali from the 14th century. The Kano Chronicle, written in Arabic, records the kings of Kano back to the 10th century.
Queen Amina of Zazzau

Hausa tradition remembers Amina, daughter of Bakwa Turunku of Zazzau, as a warrior queen of the 16th century. She is said to have led armies of thousands of horsemen, extended Zazzau's power to the Niger and Benue rivers, forced cities to pay tribute and built walled camps wherever she stopped. Earthen walls around old Hausa towns are still called ganuwar Amina, Amina's walls. She remains a powerful symbol of women's leadership in Nigeria, and a statue of her stands in Lagos.
The Sokoto Caliphate

In 1804 the Fulani Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio, who had been preaching reform in Gobir, declared a jihad against the Hausa kings, accusing them of corruption and mixing Islam with older practices. By 1808 most Hausa states had fallen, and the Sokoto Caliphate was established, one of the largest states in 19th-century Africa, with its capital at Sokoto.

The old Hausa kings were replaced by Fulani emirs, though many fled and founded new states, such as Maradi in today's Niger. The caliphate encouraged literacy and scholarship: Usman dan Fodio, his brother Abdullahi and his daughter Nana Asma'u wrote hundreds of works in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa. Nana Asma'u trained networks of women teachers called the jaji. Hausa culture absorbed the Fulani rulers, who adopted the Hausa language.
Society and religion

Hausa society is overwhelmingly Muslim, and Islam shapes daily life, law, dress and festivals. Emirs remain important traditional rulers. Society was traditionally ranked, with royalty, officials, scholars (malamai), traders and craftspeople each having their place. Craft guilds such as blacksmiths, weavers, dyers, leatherworkers and butchers passed their skills from father to son.

Before Islam, and alongside it in some communities, older beliefs survived in Bori, a spirit possession practice in which spirits are invited to heal illness. The Maguzawa are Hausa who kept these older beliefs.
Crafts: indigo, leather and architecture

The Kofar Mata dye pits in Kano, said to date back to the 15th century, are still in use: deep pits filled with indigo, ash and potash where cloth is dyed a deep blue, then beaten to a glossy shine. Hausa leather from tanned goat skin, famous as 'Moroccan leather', was carried across the Sahara to North Africa and Europe.

Hausa architecture uses mud and palm-wood beams to create cool buildings with decorated facades called zanko, horn-like pinnacles on the rooftops, and intricate relief patterns around doors. The Emir's palaces of Kano and Zaria are masterpieces of this style.
The Durbar

The Durbar, held during the Muslim festivals of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, is one of Africa's greatest spectacles. Hundreds of horsemen in brilliant robes and turbans, their horses dressed in quilted armour and coloured cloth, gallop towards the emir and stop suddenly in salute. The tradition comes from the cavalry reviews of the old emirates, when each district had to show its readiness for war. Kano, Katsina, Zaria and Bida hold the most famous durbars.
Food

Tuwo, a stiff dough of millet, sorghum or rice, is the everyday staple, eaten with miyan kuka (baobab leaf soup), miyan taushe (pumpkin soup) or miyan geda (groundnut soup). Masa are fermented rice cakes eaten with honey or spicy soup, and fura da nono is a millet ball mixed with fresh fermented milk. Suya, spicy grilled meat skewers dusted with yaji pepper and groundnut powder, began in Hausa country and is now loved across Nigeria and beyond.
Language and writing

Hausa belongs to the Chadic branch of the Afroasiatic family, making it a distant relative of Arabic, Amharic and ancient Egyptian. It is tonal and has special 'implosive' consonants written as ɓ and ɗ. For centuries Hausa was written in Ajami, the Arabic script adapted for African languages; today the Latin-based alphabet called Boko is used in schools and media. BBC Hausa, Voice of America and Deutsche Welle broadcast to millions of listeners.

Proverbs:
• 'Sannu sannu bata hana zuwa.' Slowly, slowly does not stop arrival.
• 'Komai nisan jifa, ƙasa zai dawo.' However far a stone is thrown, it falls back to the ground.
Colonial era and today

British forces under Frederick Lugard conquered the Sokoto Caliphate between 1900 and 1903, and Northern Nigeria became a protectorate ruled through the emirs under indirect rule. After independence, Hausa-Fulani politicians led by Ahmadu Bello, Sardauna of Sokoto, dominated northern politics.

Today Kano is one of Nigeria's largest cities and a commercial hub. Kannywood, the Hausa-language film industry based in Kano, produces hundreds of films a year, and Hausa music, poetry and literature, including popular Littattafan Soyayya (romance novels), have large audiences.
Did you know?

• Kano's Kurmi Market is said to have been founded in the 15th century and is one of the oldest markets in West Africa.
• Many Hausa words are used across West Africa, such as 'kawai' (only) and 'zongo', the name for strangers' quarters in Ghanaian towns.
• The Hausa emirates kept Arabic manuscripts on law, astronomy, medicine and poetry, some of which survive in libraries in Kano and Sokoto.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Akan / Ashanti
peoples.blurb: The people of gold, kente and the Golden Stool, whose Asante Empire was one of the most powerful states in West African history.
peoples.population: About 20 million people (the Akan make up nearly half of Ghana)
sections: Overview

The Akan are a group of related peoples who live in southern and central Ghana and eastern Côte d'Ivoire. They include the Asante (Ashanti), Fante, Akuapem, Akyem, Bono, Kwahu, Wassa, Baoulé and Agni, among others. Together they are the largest group in Ghana.

Akan peoples share a common heritage: related languages (Twi and Fante are the best known), a matrilineal family system, the seven-day naming system, and traditions of gold, kingship and art. The Asante built the most famous Akan state, an empire whose capital Kumasi was one of the great cities of 19th-century Africa.
Origins: Bono and the forest kingdoms

The Akan are linked to the early kingdom of Bonoman (Bono State), which grew in the woodland north of the forest around the 12th to 13th centuries and traded gold with Mande merchants from Djenné and Timbuktu. As demand for gold rose, Akan families moved into the rainforest, clearing land with the labour of enslaved and free workers and founding states such as Denkyira, Akwamu and Adansi.

Gold was everywhere in Akan life: it was mined from pits and washed from rivers, and gold dust was the everyday currency, measured with small brass weights cast in the shapes of animals, people and proverbs.
The Golden Stool and the rise of Asante

At the end of the 17th century several small Akan states around Kumasi were paying tribute to powerful Denkyira. According to tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye called down from the sky a stool covered in gold, which landed on the knees of Osei Tutu, chief of Kumasi. He declared that the Sika Dwa Kofi, the Golden Stool, held the soul (sunsum) of the Asante nation; as long as it was safe, the nation would be strong.

United under Osei Tutu as the first Asantehene (king of Asante), the Asante defeated Denkyira at the Battle of Feyiase around 1701. The Golden Stool is never sat upon, not even by the king; it rests on its own stool and is the true throne of the nation. The annual Odwira festival renewed the bonds between the king, the chiefs and the ancestors.
The Asante Empire

In the 18th and early 19th centuries the Asante expanded to rule most of modern Ghana and parts of Togo and Côte d'Ivoire, an area larger than the modern country. Kumasi had broad, clean streets, a great palace, and a highly organised government with treasury officials, messengers who carried gold-covered staffs, road-maintenance officers and a well-drilled army.

A council of chiefs, the Asanteman Council, advised the king, and the Asantehemaa, the queen mother, held great power: she helped choose the new king from among eligible royals and could warn or even remove him. Asante traded gold and kola to the north and gold and enslaved captives to European forts on the coast, in exchange for guns, cloth and salt.
Wars with Britain and Yaa Asantewaa

The Asante fought several wars with the British between 1824 and 1900. They won major victories, including at Nsamankow in 1824 where the British governor Sir Charles MacCarthy was killed. In 1874 a British force burned Kumasi, and in 1896 Britain exiled the Asantehene Prempeh I to the Seychelles.

In 1900 the British governor Frederick Hodgson demanded that the Golden Stool be brought to him so he could sit on it. This deep insult sparked the War of the Golden Stool, led by Nana Yaa Asantewaa, the queen mother of Ejisu, who rallied the chiefs with the famous words that if the men would not fight, the women would. The rebellion was crushed and she was exiled, but the British never captured the Golden Stool, which had been hidden. Prempeh I returned in 1924 and the Asante kingdom was restored in 1935.
Family and society

Akan society is matrilineal: a person belongs to their mother's abusua (clan), and property and many titles pass through the female line, often from a man to his sister's son. There are eight main abusua, such as Oyoko (the royal clan of Asante), Bretuo, Agona, Asona and Aduana. The father's line gives a person their ntoro, a spiritual inheritance linked to character.

Each chief sits on a stool, and stools are the symbol of authority: chiefs are 'enstooled' and 'destooled' rather than crowned. A chief always speaks in public through an okyeame (linguist), who holds a staff topped with a golden symbol and transmits the chief's words with poetic skill.
Names, days and the week

Akan children receive a day name according to the day of the week they were born. Boys: Kwasi (Sunday), Kwadwo (Monday), Kwabena (Tuesday), Kwaku (Wednesday), Yaw (Thursday), Kofi (Friday), Kwame (Saturday). Girls: Akosua, Adwoa, Abena, Akua, Yaa, Afua and Amma. Ghana's first president Kwame Nkrumah was a Saturday child, and Kofi Annan, former UN Secretary-General, was born on a Friday.
Kente and Adinkra

Kente is a hand-woven cloth of narrow strips sewn together, famous for its bright patterns of gold, green, red and black. Its home is Bonwire near Kumasi (Asante kente) and the Volta region (Ewe kente). Each pattern has a name and meaning, such as Adwinasa ('all motifs are used up', a sign of great skill) or Sika Futuro (gold dust). In the past certain patterns were reserved for the Asantehene.

Adinkra symbols are stamped onto cloth with carved calabash stamps and a dark dye made from tree bark. Each symbol carries a proverb or idea: Gye Nyame (except God, I fear none), Sankofa (go back and fetch it: learn from the past), Dwennimmen (ram's horns: humility and strength) and Duafe (the comb: beauty and care). Adinkra cloth was traditionally worn at funerals.
Anansi, the spider

Kweku Anansi, the clever spider, is the hero of Akan folktales. In the most famous story, Anansi buys all the stories in the world from Nyame, the sky god, by capturing the python, the leopard, the hornets and the fairy Mmoatia. Since then, stories in Akan are called anansesem, spider stories. Anansi tales travelled with enslaved Africans to Jamaica, the Caribbean and the American South, where he is known as Aunt Nancy or Mr Nancy.
Festivals and food

Major festivals include the Akwasidae, held every six weeks to honour the ancestors and the Golden Stool; Odwira, a purification festival; the Fante Fetu Afahye of Cape Coast; and Homowo, celebrated by the Ga (neighbours of the Akan) to 'hoot at hunger'.

Fufu, pounded cassava and plantain, is eaten with light soup, palm nut soup or groundnut soup. Other favourites include ampesi (boiled yam or plantain), kenkey, kelewele (spicy fried plantain) and the famous Ghanaian jollof.
Language and proverbs

Twi (Asante Twi and Akuapem Twi) and Fante are the main Akan languages, part of the Kwa branch of Niger-Congo. Akan is tonal and rich in proverbs, which elders use to show wisdom.

• 'Obi nkyerɛ abofra Nyame.' No one teaches a child about God (some things everybody knows).
• 'Tikoro nkɔ agyina.' One head does not hold council (two heads are better than one).
• 'Sɛ wo werɛ fi na wosan kɔfa a yenkyi.' It is not wrong to go back for what you forgot (the meaning of Sankofa).
Colonial era and today

The Gold Coast became a British colony, and Kumasi was occupied in 1896. In 1957 the Gold Coast became Ghana, the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence, under Kwame Nkrumah, a Nzema (an Akan-related people). The Golden Stool still sits at the Manhyia Palace in Kumasi, where the Asantehene, Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, reigns as a highly respected traditional ruler. Ghana remains one of the world's leading producers of gold and cocoa, both crops of Akan lands.
Did you know?

• Akan brass gold weights number in the hundreds of thousands in museum collections and often depict proverbs.
• The black star on Ghana's flag and the national football team's name, the Black Stars, honour African freedom.
• Kente cloth is often worn by African Americans at graduations as a symbol of heritage.

peoples.name: Mandinka
peoples.region: Mali, Guinea, The Gambia, Senegal and Guinea-Bissau
peoples.blurb: Heirs of Sundiata Keita and the Mali Empire, keepers of the kora and the griot tradition, and authors of one of the world's first human-rights charters.
peoples.population: About 11 million Mandinka, part of a Mande world of more than 40 million
sections: Overview

The Mandinka (also called Malinke or Mandingo) are a Mande people of West Africa. They live in Mali, Guinea, The Gambia, Senegal, Guinea-Bissau and Côte d'Ivoire, and are closely related to the Bambara and Dyula. Their homeland, Manden, lies on the upper Niger near the border of Mali and Guinea.

The Mandinka are famous as the founders of the Mali Empire, as traders who spread Islam and commerce across West Africa, and as the keepers of a great oral tradition preserved by griots.
Sundiata and the founding of Mali

In the early 13th century the Manden was ruled by Sumanguru Kanté, the sorcerer-king of the Sosso. According to the Epic of Sundiata, a crippled boy named Sundiata (also Sunjata or Sogolon Jara), son of a king and of Sogolon the buffalo woman, overcame mockery to walk at last, holding an iron bar that bent like a bow. Exiled by jealous rivals, he grew into a mighty warrior.

The Mandinka chiefs called him home, and around 1235 Sundiata defeated Sumanguru at the Battle of Kirina. He became mansa (king of kings) and united the clans into the Mali Empire. The epic, recited by griots to this day, is one of the great heroic poems of the world.
The Kurukan Fuga charter

After Kirina, according to tradition, Sundiata and his allies met at Kurukan Fuga and proclaimed rules for the new empire: the division of society into clans, the rights and duties of each, respect for women, protection of strangers, the forbidding of mistreatment of enslaved people, and the 'joking relationships' (sanankuya) between clans that defuse conflict with humour.

The Manden Charter, proclaimed in Kurukan Fuga, was recognised by UNESCO in 2009 as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, and it is often described as one of the oldest constitutions and human-rights declarations in the world.
Mansa Musa and the golden age

Mali reached its height under Mansa Musa (reigned about 1312 to 1337). In 1324 he made the pilgrimage to Mecca with a caravan said to include thousands of people and camels carrying gold. In Cairo he gave away so much gold that its value fell for years. He returned with scholars and the architect Abu Ishaq es-Saheli, who is credited with designing mosques at Gao and Timbuktu, including the Djinguereber Mosque.

Under Musa, Mali stretched from the Atlantic coast to beyond the Niger bend, controlling the gold of Bambuk and Bure and the trans-Saharan trade. Timbuktu became a great centre of learning. The traveller Ibn Battuta visited Mali in 1352 and praised its safety and justice, writing that a traveller had nothing to fear from thieves. In 1375 Mansa Musa appeared on the Catalan Atlas, a European map, holding a golden nugget.
Decline and later history

From the 15th century Mali weakened as Songhai rose in the east and provinces broke away. Mandinka traders and warriors moved west, founding the kingdom of Kaabu in Guinea-Bissau and Senegambia. In the 19th century the Mandinka leader Samori Touré built the Wassoulou Empire and fought the French for almost twenty years before his capture in 1898.
Society and the griots

Mandinka society was traditionally divided into the horon (free-born nobles and farmers), the nyamakala (specialised craft groups) and the jon (enslaved or captive people). The nyamakala include blacksmiths (numu), leatherworkers (garanke) and griots (jeli).

The jeli is a living library: a musician, historian, genealogist and adviser who memorises the history of families, the epic of Sundiata and the deeds of kings. A famous saying holds that 'when a griot dies, a library burns'. Griot families such as the Kouyaté, descended from Sundiata's griot Balla Fasséké, pass knowledge from parent to child. Kings were never without their griot.
Music: the kora and balafon

The kora is a 21-stringed harp-lute made from a large calabash covered with cowhide, played with the thumbs and index fingers. Its shimmering sound is the voice of Mandinka music. Master players include Toumani Diabaté of Mali, whose family has played the kora for 71 generations, and Sona Jobarteh of The Gambia, the first woman to become a professional kora virtuoso from a griot family.

The balafon, a wooden xylophone with calabash resonators, is even older: the Sosso Bala, said to have belonged to Sumanguru himself, is kept in Niagassola, Guinea, and was recognised by UNESCO in 2001.
Religion and daily life

Most Mandinka have been Muslim for centuries, and Mandinka traders (Dyula) helped spread Islam across West Africa. Older beliefs survive in respect for ancestors, protective amulets and initiation societies such as the hunters' brotherhood (donso), whose songs and rituals are also UNESCO-listed.

Village life revolves around farming millet, sorghum, rice and groundnuts. Circumcision and initiation mark the passage to adulthood, and names are given at a naming ceremony seven days after birth.
Language

Mandinka belongs to the Mande branch of the Niger-Congo family. The related Manding languages, Bambara, Malinke, Dyula and Mandinka, are largely mutually understandable and are spoken by tens of millions. In 1949 the Guinean scholar Solomana Kanté invented the N'Ko alphabet to write Manding languages, and it is used today in books, newspapers and on phones.

Proverb: 'Ni i ma se ka kuma, i bɛ se ka lamɛn.' If you cannot speak, you can listen.
Colonial era and today

The Mandinka lands were divided between France (Mali, Guinea, Senegal), Britain (The Gambia) and Portugal (Guinea-Bissau). Mandinka people played key roles in independence and national life; Sékou Touré, Guinea's first president, claimed descent from Samori Touré. The Mandinka of The Gambia became world famous through Alex Haley's Roots (1976), which traced his ancestor Kunta Kinte to the village of Juffureh.
Did you know?

• The modern country of Mali takes its name from the medieval empire.
• The word 'Mandinka' means 'people of Manden'.
• The ruins of Niani, in Guinea, are thought by many historians to be one of the capitals of the Mali Empire.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Wolof
peoples.blurb: Founders of the Jolof Empire, masters of teranga hospitality and of mbalax music, whose language unites modern Senegal.
peoples.population: About 6 to 7 million native speakers; spoken by most Senegalese
sections: Overview

The Wolof are the largest ethnic group in Senegal and are also found in The Gambia and southern Mauritania. Their language is the everyday language of Senegal: in Dakar, people of every background speak Wolof at home, in the market and on the radio.

Wolof culture is famous for teranga, the spirit of hospitality: guests are welcomed, fed and treated with generosity. Senegal calls itself 'the land of teranga', and its national football team is the 'Lions of Teranga'.
The Jolof Empire

According to tradition, the Wolof state was founded by the legendary Ndiadiane Ndiaye, a mysterious figure who appeared from the waters of a lake in Waalo and settled a dispute between villagers so wisely that they made him king. The Jolof Empire grew from the 14th century (traditions date its founding to around 1350) and united the Wolof kingdoms of Waalo, Kayor, Baol and Sine and Saloum under the Buurba Jolof.

In 1549, at the Battle of Danki, Amari Ngoné Sobel Fall of Kayor defeated the Buurba Jolof, and the empire broke into independent kingdoms: Jolof, Waalo, Kayor and Baol. The coastal kingdoms grew rich through trade with the Portuguese, French and English.
The kingdoms and their heroes

Each kingdom had its own ruler: the Damel of Kayor, the Brak of Waalo, the Teigne of Baol. Rulers were chosen by councils of nobles from royal lineages, and powerful queens and royal women (linguère) wielded real influence.

In the 19th century Lat Dior Diop, Damel of Kayor, resisted the French and their railway from Dakar to Saint-Louis, dying in battle at Dekheulé in 1886. He is a Senegalese national hero. In Waalo, Queen Ndaté Yalla Mbodj fought French expansion in the 1840s and 1850s.
Society

Traditional Wolof society was ranked. The geer were free-born nobles and farmers; the ñeeño were craft castes such as smiths (tëgg), leatherworkers (uude) and griots (gewel); and the jaam were enslaved people. Though these divisions have faded, they still sometimes influence marriage.

The gewel, the Wolof griots, are praise singers, historians and musicians, and the sabar drummers are among the most celebrated performers in Senegal.
Religion and the brotherhoods

Most Wolof are Muslim and belong to Sufi brotherhoods (tariqa). The Mouride brotherhood was founded by Sheikh Amadou Bamba (1853 to 1927), who preached peaceful resistance to French rule, work and devotion. The French exiled him to Gabon and Mauritania, but his following only grew. Every year millions of pilgrims travel to Touba for the Grand Magal, commemorating his exile. The Tijaniyya, centred in Tivaouane, is the other great brotherhood.

The brotherhoods play a huge role in Senegalese life, economy and politics. A famous Mouride saying is 'work as if you will never die, pray as if you will die tomorrow'.
Music and wrestling

Mbalax is Senegal's popular music, blending sabar drumming with guitars, keyboards and Cuban rhythms. Youssou N'Dour, a Wolof singer from the Medina in Dakar, made mbalax famous worldwide; his song with Neneh Cherry, '7 Seconds', became a global hit in 1994.

Laamb, Senegalese wrestling with punches, is the national sport. Champions such as Tyson, Yékini and Balla Gaye 2 are national celebrities, and big fights fill stadiums, accompanied by drumming, poetry and protective charms.
Food

Thieboudienne (ceebu jën), rice cooked in a rich tomato sauce with fish and vegetables, is Senegal's national dish and was recognised by UNESCO in 2021. Other favourites include yassa (chicken or fish with onions and lemon), mafé (groundnut stew), and thiakry (millet with sweet yoghurt). Attaya, strong green mint tea poured from high to make foam and served in three rounds, is a social ritual: the first round is bitter like death, the second sweet like life, the third sweet like love.
Language

Wolof belongs to the Atlantic branch of Niger-Congo. Unlike most of its neighbours, it is not tonal. It was historically written in Ajami (Arabic script), called Wolofal, and today uses the Latin alphabet. French-Wolof mixing, 'urban Wolof', is the speech of Dakar.

Proverbs:
• 'Ndank ndank mooy japp golo ci ñaay.' Slowly, slowly, one catches the monkey in the forest.
• 'Nit nitay garabam.' A person is another person's medicine (people need each other).
Colonial era and today

Saint-Louis, founded by the French in 1659, became the capital of French West Africa, and Gorée Island off Dakar is a UNESCO site remembering the Atlantic slave trade. The 'Four Communes' gave some Africans French citizenship and elected Blaise Diagne as the first Black African in the French parliament in 1914. Senegal became independent in 1960 under Léopold Sédar Senghor, a Serer poet. Today Wolof is the heart of Senegalese identity, music, film and comedy.
Did you know?

• The word 'banana' may come from Wolof, via Portuguese traders.
• 'Dëgg' (truth) is often linked by some writers to the English slang 'dig', meaning understand.
• Senegal's 'Lions of Teranga' won the Africa Cup of Nations in 2022.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Fulani
peoples.region: Across the Sahel, from Senegal to Sudan
peoples.blurb: The great herders of the Sahel, spread across more than 20 countries, founders of jihad states and keepers of the code of pulaaku.
sections: Overview

The Fulani (Fulɓe, Peul in French) are one of the most widely spread peoples in Africa, living in some twenty countries from Senegal and Mauritania in the west to Sudan and the Central African Republic in the east. Many are pastoralists who move with their cattle in search of water and grass; others are settled farmers, traders and city dwellers.

Wherever they live, the Fulani are united by their language, Fula, by cattle and by pulaaku, a moral code of patience, self-control, modesty and dignity.
Origins

The origins of the Fulani are debated. Linguistically, Fula is closely related to Wolof and Serer of Senegal, suggesting the Fulani emerged in the Senegal river valley, in Futa Toro, perhaps among the people of the ancient kingdom of Tekrur. Rock paintings in the Sahara, such as those at Tassili n'Ajjer, show cattle herders, and some researchers link them to Fulani ancestors.

From around the 11th century onward Fulani herders gradually spread east across the Sahel, settling in Macina (Mali), Hausaland, Adamawa (Cameroon) and beyond, often living alongside farming peoples and exchanging milk for grain.
The jihad states

From the 18th century Fulani Muslim scholars led a series of reform movements that created powerful states. In Fouta Djallon (Guinea) a theocratic state formed around 1725, led by an almamy. In Futa Toro (Senegal) a revolution in 1776 created another. The greatest was the Sokoto Caliphate, founded by Usman dan Fodio after his jihad of 1804, which ruled much of northern Nigeria, Niger and Cameroon.

In 1818 Seku Amadu founded the Massina Empire in the inner Niger delta of Mali, with Hamdullahi as its capital, and in the mid-19th century the Tukulor leader El Hadj Umar Tall built an empire stretching from Senegal to Timbuktu.
Pastoral life and cattle

For pastoral Fulani, cattle are wealth, identity and love. The famous long-horned Zebu breeds such as the red Bororo (Mbororo) cattle are prized. A herder knows each cow by name and history. Seasonal movement, transhumance, follows the rains: north in the wet season, south in the dry season.

Milk is central to the diet, and selling milk and butter is traditionally the work of women. Herding today faces serious challenges from climate change, the loss of grazing land to farms and towns, and violent conflict between herders and farmers in several countries.
Pulaaku: the Fulani way

Pulaaku means 'Fulani-ness', the qualities a true Pullo should have: munyal (patience and self-control), semteende (modesty and reserve), hakkille (wisdom and forethought) and sagata (courage). A Fulani person should not show hunger, pain or strong emotion in public. Elders say that pulaaku is what separates a Pullo from others more than language or cattle.
Festivals and ceremonies

The Wodaabe, a nomadic Fulani group of Niger and Chad, hold the Gerewol at the end of the rainy season. Young men paint their faces with yellow clay and black kohl, wear ostrich feathers and beads, and perform the yaake dance, rolling their eyes and showing their white teeth, while young women judge the most beautiful.

In parts of Nigeria and Niger the sharo, a test of manhood, sees young men endure whipping in public without flinching, to show bravery and earn the right to marry. The Dewgal festival in Mali celebrates the crossing of the Niger river by herds returning from the dry season pastures.
Dress and art

Fulani women are known for their elaborate hairstyles, braided crests and amber, coins and silver ornaments, large gold earrings among the Fulani of Mali, and facial tattoos around the mouth. Men wear wide-brimmed conical hats made of leather and straw. Fulani blankets woven of wool in geometric patterns, such as the khasa of Mali, are prized across the Sahel.
Language

Fula (also called Fulfulde, Pulaar or Pular) belongs to the Atlantic branch of Niger-Congo and has many dialects across its huge range. It is famous among linguists for its system of around 20 noun classes and for consonant mutation, where the first sound of a word changes with its grammar. It was written in Ajami for centuries and in 1989 two Guinean brothers, Ibrahima and Abdoulaye Barry, invented the Adlam alphabet, now supported on smartphones.

Proverb: 'Si a yahii hoore nden a yiiat ngaal.' If you go far, you will see a horn (travel brings knowledge).
Today

Fulani people are prominent in politics, religion, business and the arts across West Africa. Nigeria's president Muhammadu Buhari (2015 to 2023) and Senegal's president Macky Sall (2012 to 2024) are of Fulani heritage. Fulani music by artists such as Baaba Maal of Senegal and Oumou Sangaré's collaborators has reached global audiences.
Did you know?

• The word 'Fulani' comes from Hausa; the people call themselves Fulɓe (plural) and Pullo (singular).
• Fulani herders have helped spread zebu cattle across vast parts of Africa.
• Fouta Djallon, a Fulani heartland, is called the water tower of West Africa because the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers rise there.

peoples.name: Kikuyu
peoples.blurb: Farmers of the highlands around Mount Kenya, children of Gikuyu and Mumbi, and central figures in Kenya's fight for freedom.
peoples.population: About 8 million people, Kenya's largest ethnic group
sections: Overview

The Kikuyu (Agĩkũyũ) are the largest ethnic group in Kenya, living mainly in the fertile highlands of central Kenya around Mount Kenya, in counties such as Kiambu, Murang'a, Nyeri, Kirinyaga and Nyandarua, and in large numbers in Nairobi and the Rift Valley.

The Kikuyu are a Bantu people, traditionally farmers who grew millet, sorghum, beans, yams and later maize, coffee and tea, while also keeping goats, sheep and cattle. They are known for enterprise, education and their central role in Kenya's struggle for independence.
Gikuyu and Mumbi

The Kikuyu origin story tells that Ngai (God), who lives on the snowy peak of Mount Kenya, Kĩrĩnyaga ('the mountain of brightness'), took the first man, Gikuyu, to the top of the mountain and showed him the beautiful land. He gave Gikuyu a place by a grove of fig trees, Mukurwe wa Nyagathanga, and a wife, Mumbi, 'the creator' or 'moulder'.

They had nine daughters but no sons. Gikuyu prayed under a sacred fig tree, and nine young men appeared, who married the daughters. The nine daughters founded the nine main Kikuyu clans (mbari), such as Anjiru, Ambui, Aceera and Agaciku, which is why the clans carry women's names. A tenth clan is often mentioned, representing extra daughters. For this reason Kikuyu people still call themselves 'the house of Mumbi', nyũmba ya Mumbi.
Migration and early history

Historians believe the ancestors of the Kikuyu came from the north-east, moving with other Thagicu peoples (such as the Meru, Embu and Kamba) into the Mount Kenya region from around the 16th century or earlier. They cleared the dense highland forests for farming, sometimes buying land from the Gumba and Athi hunting peoples who lived there before them.

They traded with neighbours: food and tobacco to the Maasai in exchange for livestock and skins, and goods with the Kamba, who linked them to Swahili traders on the coast. Intermarriage with the Maasai was common, and the two peoples share some customs.
Government and age sets

The Kikuyu had no king. Authority came from councils of elders, kiama, at the level of the ridge, village and wider district. A man moved through stages of life by initiation: boyhood, warrior (mũthũri wa njamba), junior elder and senior elder, with each stage bringing new rights and duties.

Every generation was part of an age set, and power passed between two great generation groups, Mwangi and Maina, in a ceremony called ituĩka, held roughly every 25 to 40 years, when the ruling generation handed over to the next. The last full ituĩka took place in the late 19th century; colonial authorities stopped the one planned for the 1920s.
Religion

The Kikuyu believed in one God, Ngai or Mwene-Nyaga, the owner of brightness, who lived on Mount Kenya. Prayers and sacrifices were offered facing the mountain, and sacred fig trees (mũgumo) were places of worship and community gatherings. Ancestral spirits were honoured and their displeasure feared. Today most Kikuyu are Christian, but respect for Mount Kenya and the mũgumo tree remains part of cultural identity.
Land and family

Land is at the heart of Kikuyu life. Family land, githaka, was held by lineages and passed down through generations. Homesteads (mũciĩ) had a hut for the husband and separate huts for each wife and her children, with granaries and animal pens.

Marriage involved negotiations and the payment of ruracio, bride wealth, in goats and other gifts, which joined two families together. Ceremonies such as ngurario, the final wedding rite, are still held today in modern form.
Colonialism and the land question

When the British built the Uganda Railway and settled the 'White Highlands' in the early 20th century, they took large areas of the best Kikuyu land for European farms. Many Kikuyu became squatters on land that had been theirs, or were pushed into crowded reserves. Taxes, forced labour and the kipande identity pass deepened resentment.

Kikuyu political organisations grew from the 1920s, including the Kikuyu Central Association, of which Jomo Kenyatta became secretary. Kenyatta's book Facing Mount Kenya (1938) was one of the first works of anthropology written by an African about his own people.
The Mau Mau uprising

In the early 1950s the Land and Freedom Army, known as Mau Mau, launched an armed struggle against colonial rule, mostly among the Kikuyu, Embu and Meru. Fighters took oaths of unity and lived in the forests of Mount Kenya and the Aberdares under leaders such as Dedan Kimathi.

The British declared a state of emergency in 1952. Tens of thousands of Kenyans were killed and hundreds of thousands were detained in camps, where many suffered torture. Dedan Kimathi was captured and hanged in 1957. In 2013 the British government expressed regret and paid compensation to over 5,000 surviving victims of abuse. The uprising was defeated militarily, but it made colonial rule impossible to sustain.
Independence and today

Kenya became independent in 1963, and Jomo Kenyatta was its first prime minister and then president until 1978. His son Uhuru Kenyatta was president from 2013 to 2022, and Mwai Kibaki, also Kikuyu, from 2002 to 2013.

Wangari Maathai, a Kikuyu scientist from Nyeri, founded the Green Belt Movement, which planted tens of millions of trees, and in 2004 became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. The writer Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o famously chose to write novels and plays in Gĩkũyũ rather than English. Today Kikuyu people are prominent in business, farming, education and the arts.
Food

Githeri, maize and beans boiled together, is the classic Kikuyu meal. Mũkimo (or irio) is mashed potatoes with green peas, maize and pumpkin leaves, often served with nyama choma (roasted meat). Ũcũrũ is a fermented porridge of millet or maize, and mũratina was a traditional honey beer used in ceremonies.
Language and proverbs

Gĩkũyũ is a Bantu language closely related to Embu, Meru and Kamba. It is written with the Latin alphabet with the special letters ĩ and ũ.

• 'Gũtirĩ ũtukũ ũtakĩa.' There is no night that does not end in dawn.
• 'Kĩrĩra kĩa mũthuri ti kĩa mũndũ mũrũme.' A man's secret is not shared with everyone.
• 'Mũthenya ũmwe ndũũmaga ũrũmwe.' One day does not dry the gourd (patience).
Did you know?

• Mount Kenya took its name from the Kamba pronunciation 'Kiinyaa' of the Kikuyu 'Kĩrĩnyaga'.
• Nyeri, a Kikuyu town, is where Lord Baden-Powell, founder of the Scouts, is buried.
• The Kikuyu name Wanjiru comes from the Anjiru clan, one of the nine daughters' clans.
Sources and further reading
Jomo Kenyatta, Facing Mount Kenya (1938); Caroline Elkins, Imperial Reckoning; Wikipedia: Kikuyu people, Mau Mau rebellion, Wangari Maathai; Nobel Prize: Wangari Maathai biography (2004).

peoples.name: Maasai
peoples.blurb: Semi-nomadic herders of the Great Rift Valley, famous for their red shúkà, leaping dances and the belief that all cattle were given to them by God.
sections: Overview

The Maasai live in southern Kenya and northern Tanzania, across the grasslands of the Great Rift Valley, including the Maasai Mara, the Serengeti, the Ngorongoro highlands and the plains around Mount Kilimanjaro. They are a Nilotic people who speak Maa, and they are among the best-known peoples of Africa thanks to their striking dress, beadwork and close relationship with cattle and wildlife.

Traditionally the Maasai are semi-nomadic pastoralists, moving their herds of cattle, goats and sheep between seasonal pastures and water.
Origins and history

Maasai oral history says they came from the lower Nile valley, north-west of Lake Turkana, migrating south from around the 15th century. By the 18th and 19th centuries they controlled a vast territory from northern Kenya to central Tanzania, and their warriors were feared by caravans and neighbours alike.

The late 19th century brought disaster, known as the emutai: rinderpest killed up to 90 per cent of their cattle, followed by drought, smallpox and famine. Then British treaties in 1904 and 1911 pushed the Kenyan Maasai off much of their best land, including the Laikipia plateau, into a southern reserve. Later, national parks such as the Serengeti and game reserves took more of their grazing land.
Cattle and God

Cattle are at the centre of Maasai life and belief. The Maasai believe that Enkai (also Engai), God, gave all the cattle on earth to them at the beginning of time. A Maasai man's wealth and status are measured in cattle and children.

Cattle provide milk, meat, blood, hides for bedding and dung for plastering houses. Blood, drawn from a cow's neck with a blunted arrow without killing it, is drunk mixed with milk, especially by warriors, by women after childbirth and by the sick. A traditional greeting asks about cattle and children before anything else.
Age sets and the warriors

Maasai society is organised by age sets. Boys are circumcised in their teens and become il-murran, warriors, responsible for protecting the community and its herds. Each age set is given a name and its members are bonded for life. Warriors traditionally lived together in a special camp called a manyatta, grew their hair long and dyed it with red ochre.

After about ten to fifteen years warriors pass through the Eunoto ceremony, in which their mothers shave their long hair and they become junior elders, allowed to marry and to start their own families. Elders make decisions through discussion, and a spiritual leader, the laibon, interprets omens, offers healing and advises on ceremonies.
Homes and family

A Maasai homestead, enkang (often called a boma or manyatta), is a circle of low, loaf-shaped houses built by women from a frame of poles plastered with mud, cow dung and urine. An outer fence of thorn bushes protects people and animals, and cattle are brought into the central enclosure at night.

Men may have more than one wife, and each wife has her own house. Children belong to the whole community, and grandparents play a big part in raising them.
Dress and beadwork

The red shúkà, a cloth wrapped around the body, is the most recognisable Maasai garment; red is thought to frighten lions and symbolise bravery and blood. Blue, purple and checked patterns are also popular.

Beadwork, made by women, is a language of its own. Each colour has a meaning: red for bravery and unity, blue for the sky and God's rain, green for land and growth, white for milk and purity, orange and yellow for hospitality, and black for the struggles of life. Collars, earrings and headbands tell others about a person's age, marital status and position.
Adumu: the jumping dance

The adumu, often called the jumping dance, is performed during the Eunoto ceremony and other celebrations. Warriors form a circle and take turns to leap high into the air from a standing position, keeping their bodies straight and heels never touching each other, while the others sing in deep throaty harmonies. The higher the jump, the greater the warrior's reputation, and it can impress future wives.
Land, wildlife and change

The Maasai have lived alongside lions, elephants, wildebeest and giraffes for centuries; because they rarely hunt wild animals for food, wildlife survives in great numbers on their lands. Today many Maasai communities run wildlife conservancies and lodges around the Maasai Mara, earning income from tourism while protecting habitat.

Yet the Maasai face serious pressure. Land has been lost to farms, towns and parks, and in Tanzania there have been painful disputes over evictions in Loliondo and the Ngorongoro Conservation Area. Climate change brings longer droughts that kill livestock. Many young Maasai now go to school and work in cities, while trying to keep their culture alive.
Language and proverbs

Maa is a Nilotic language, related to Samburu and Turkana. It is tonal.

• 'Meeta enkima nemeeta osupuko.' There is no hill without a valley.
• 'Eng'eno o lkulie, nemeeta.' Wisdom is like the shell of a tortoise: everyone carries their own.
• 'Meishoo iyiook enkai inkishu o-nkera.' May God give us cattle and children (a common blessing).
Food

The traditional Maasai diet is built on milk (kule), often fermented in calabashes cleaned with ash; meat, eaten especially at ceremonies; and blood mixed with milk. Today maize porridge (ugali), beans and tea with milk and sugar are also everyday foods.
Did you know?

• Maasai Mara National Reserve is named after the Maasai and the Mara river; 'mara' means spotted in Maa, describing the patchwork landscape.
• Maasai runners and warriors are famous for endurance, and some Maasai have competed in long-distance running.
• Each Maasai age set has a name, and people often remember history by which age set was warriors at the time.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Baganda
peoples.blurb: The people of the Kingdom of Buganda on the shores of Lake Victoria, ruled for centuries by the Kabaka, and the heart of modern Uganda.
peoples.population: About 6 to 7 million people, Uganda's largest ethnic group
sections: Overview

The Baganda (singular Muganda) are the largest ethnic group in Uganda. They live in the Kingdom of Buganda, on the northern and western shores of Lake Victoria, which includes the capital Kampala. Their language, Luganda, is widely spoken across Uganda.

Buganda is one of the oldest and best-organised kingdoms in East Africa. The country of Uganda takes its name from Buganda, through the Swahili form 'Uganda'.
Kintu and the founding of the kingdom

Baganda tradition tells that the first man on earth was Kintu, who arrived with a single cow. He married Nambi, the daughter of Ggulu, the king of heaven. Nambi's brother Walumbe (Death) followed them to earth, and that is why people die; Kintu and Nambi's children multiplied to fill the land.

Another tradition remembers Kintu as the founding king, and Kato Kimera as the first Kabaka of the royal dynasty. The kingdom is believed to have been founded around the 14th century, starting as a small state between larger neighbours such as Bunyoro-Kitara, and gradually expanding through war and diplomacy.
The Kabaka and government

The king of Buganda is the Kabaka. He ruled with the Lukiiko, a council of chiefs, and the Katikkiro, a prime minister. The kingdom was divided into counties (amasaza), each led by a chief appointed by the Kabaka, which made Buganda highly centralised: chiefs held their positions because of the king's favour, not inheritance.

Buganda society is organised into around 50 clans (ebika), each with a totem animal or plant, such as the lion, leopard, lungfish, monkey or mushroom, which members must not eat. Clans have specific roles at the royal court; for example, some clans provide royal drummers or guard the royal fire. The Kabaka himself has no clan of his own, because he belongs to all clans: princes take the clan of their mother.

The Queen Mother (Namasole) and the Queen Sister (Lubuga) held important offices and their own estates.
Expansion and the 19th century

In the 18th and 19th centuries Buganda grew into the strongest kingdom of the region, raiding neighbours and trading ivory and enslaved people for cloth and guns. Its large fleet of war canoes controlled much of Lake Victoria.

Kabaka Mutesa I (reigned about 1856 to 1884) welcomed Arab traders from Zanzibar, then the explorers John Hanning Speke (1862) and Henry Morton Stanley (1875). Stanley's appeal for missionaries brought Anglicans in 1877 and Catholic White Fathers in 1879. Mutesa skilfully played Muslims, Protestants and Catholics against one another.
The Uganda Martyrs

Mutesa's son, Kabaka Mwanga II, came to fear that Christian converts were more loyal to their new faith and to Europeans than to him. Between 1885 and 1887 he ordered the execution of many converts, both Catholic and Anglican; the most famous were burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886. Twenty-two Catholic martyrs were canonised as saints by Pope Paul VI in 1964.

Every year on 3 June, Martyrs' Day, millions of pilgrims from across Africa walk to the Namugongo shrine, one of the largest religious gatherings on the continent.
Colonial rule and independence

After religious civil wars, Britain made Buganda a protectorate in 1894, and the Buganda Agreement of 1900 gave Baganda chiefs freehold land (mailo land) and a privileged position within the Uganda Protectorate. In 1953 the British exiled Kabaka Mutesa II for refusing to merge Buganda fully into a unified Uganda, but he returned in triumph in 1955.

At independence in 1962, Mutesa II became the first president of Uganda, with Milton Obote as prime minister. In 1966 Obote's government attacked the Kabaka's palace at Mengo; Mutesa II fled to exile in London, where he died in 1969, and the kingdoms were abolished in 1967. In 1993 President Yoweri Museveni restored the traditional kingdoms as cultural institutions, and Ronald Muwenda Mutebi II was crowned the 36th Kabaka.
The Kasubi Tombs

The Tombs of the Buganda Kings at Kasubi, on a hill in Kampala, hold the remains of four Kabakas: Mutesa I, Mwanga II, Daudi Chwa II and Mutesa II. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, is a huge round house built of wooden poles, reeds and thatch, a masterpiece of Ganda architecture. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.

In March 2010 a fire destroyed the main building. It has been carefully rebuilt by traditional craftspeople from the clans responsible for the work, an effort that also revived old building skills.
Bark cloth and crafts

Bark cloth (olubugo) is made from the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree. The bark is stripped, soaked and beaten with grooved wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, wide, terracotta-coloured cloth. It was worn by kings and commoners, used in burials and ceremonies, and is still used for cultural events. Barkcloth making in Uganda was recognised by UNESCO in 2008, one of the first items on its list.

The Baganda are also known for drums: the Kabaka's royal drums (mujaguzo) are treated as sacred, and the drum-making village of Mpambire is famous.
Food and daily life

Matooke, green cooking bananas steamed in banana leaves and mashed, is the heart of Baganda food, eaten with groundnut sauce, beef, fish or beans. Luwombo is a festive dish of chicken or meat stewed in banana leaf parcels, once reserved for royalty. The banana plant is so important that there are dozens of words for its varieties and uses.

The kanzu, a long white robe, is the traditional dress for men, and the gomesi (busuuti), a floor-length dress with puffed shoulders and a sash, for women.
Language and proverbs

Luganda is a Bantu language with tones and long vowels, written with the Latin alphabet. It is widely spoken in Kampala and used in radio, music and film.

• 'Akwata empola atuuka wala.' The one who goes slowly reaches far.
• 'Amagezi ssabo, buli omu agalina.' Wisdom is like a shrine: everyone has their own.
• 'Ekyuma ky'olina kye kikutuusa.' The tool you have is the one that gets you there.
Did you know?

• The Kabaka's palace at Mengo and the Bulange (parliament) are linked by the Kabaka Anjagala road, a straight royal mile.
• Each Baganda clan has two totems, a main one (omuziro) and a secondary one (akabbiro).
• Lake Victoria is called Nnalubaale in Luganda, 'mother of the gods'.
Sources and further reading

UNESCO World Heritage: Tombs of Buganda Kings at Kasubi (2001); UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Barkcloth making in Uganda (2008); Wikipedia: Buganda, Mutesa I, Uganda Martyrs; Richard Reid, Political Power in Pre-Colonial Buganda.

peoples.name: Zulu
peoples.blurb: The 'people of heaven', united by Shaka into a powerful kingdom, famous for courage at Isandlwana, beadwork and the Reed Dance.
peoples.population: About 14 million people; isiZulu is South Africa's most spoken home language
sections: Overview

The Zulu (amaZulu) are the largest ethnic group in South Africa. Most live in KwaZulu-Natal, between the Drakensberg mountains and the Indian Ocean, and many more live in Gauteng around Johannesburg. isiZulu is the most widely spoken home language in South Africa, understood by about half the population.

The name Zulu means 'heaven' or 'sky', and amaZulu are 'the people of heaven'. They are part of the Nguni group of Bantu-speaking peoples, together with the Xhosa, Swazi and Ndebele.
Origins

The Zulu trace their name to Zulu kaMalandela, the founder of a small clan who lived in the 17th century near the White Mfolozi river. For generations the Zulu were one of many Nguni chiefdoms, raising cattle and growing sorghum and millet in the rolling hills of the region.

By the late 18th century, competition for land, trade and cattle, possibly made worse by drought, led to the rise of larger states such as the Mthethwa under Dingiswayo and the Ndwandwe under Zwide.
Shaka and the Zulu Kingdom

Shaka kaSenzangakhona was born around 1787, the son of the Zulu chief Senzangakhona and Nandi, a woman of the Langeni. Rejected by his father, he grew up in hardship and later served as a warrior under Dingiswayo of the Mthethwa. In 1816, with Dingiswayo's support, he took the Zulu chieftaincy.

Shaka transformed warfare in the region. He is credited with introducing the short stabbing spear (iklwa), the large cowhide shield, and the 'bull's horns' formation, in which the chest of the army pinned the enemy while the horns surrounded them. Regiments (amabutho) of young men of the same age lived in military towns, and discipline was strict. After defeating Zwide's Ndwandwe around 1819, Shaka built a kingdom that dominated the region.

Shaka's wars and those of other states caused great upheaval across southern Africa, sometimes called the Mfecane ('crushing'); groups such as the Ndebele of Mzilikazi and the Ngoni moved far to the north. Historians today debate how much of this disruption was caused by Shaka alone. Shaka was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana.
The Zulu and the Boers

Dingane, Shaka's successor, faced the arrival of Voortrekkers, Boer settlers moving inland from the Cape. In 1838 he killed the Boer leader Piet Retief and his party, and later that year the Boers defeated a Zulu army at the Battle of Blood River (Ncome) on 16 December. Dingane was overthrown by his brother Mpande, who ruled for over thirty years. The British created the colony of Natal in 1843.
Isandlwana and the Anglo-Zulu War

In 1879, under King Cetshwayo, the Zulu kingdom was invaded by Britain after an ultimatum that no king could accept. On 22 January 1879, at Isandlwana, a Zulu army of about 20,000 warriors overwhelmed a British camp, killing more than 1,300 soldiers: one of the worst defeats of the British army in colonial history. That same night, a small British garrison held off Zulu attacks at Rorke's Drift.

Britain sent reinforcements and defeated the Zulu at Ulundi in July 1879. Cetshwayo was captured and the kingdom was divided into thirteen chiefdoms, leading to civil war. Zululand was annexed by Britain in 1887 and joined to Natal in 1897. The Bambatha Rebellion of 1906 against poll taxes was the last armed uprising.
Society and the homestead

The traditional Zulu homestead, umuzi, is a circle of beehive-shaped huts (iqhugwane) built of grass and saplings around a central cattle enclosure, the isibaya, the most sacred place, where men gather and ancestors are honoured. The great hut of the senior wife faces the entrance.

Cattle carry wealth, honour and spiritual meaning. Lobola, the bride wealth traditionally paid in cattle, joins two families. Respect, hlonipha, shapes behaviour: married women traditionally avoid speaking words that sound like the names of their in-laws.
Religion and the ancestors

Zulu tradition recognises uMvelinqangi ('the one who came first') or uNkulunkulu, the creator, and gives great importance to the amadlozi, the ancestors, who guide and protect the living. Diviners, izangoma, communicate with ancestors through dreams and rituals, and herbalists, izinyanga, heal with plants. Most Zulu today are Christian, many in African independent churches such as the Shembe Nazareth Baptist Church, which blends Christianity with Zulu tradition.
Beadwork, dress and the Reed Dance

Zulu beadwork is a language of colour. A young woman might send a young man a beaded 'love letter' (ucu), where white means purity and love, red means passion or longing, and black can mean marriage or sorrow, depending on the pattern.

Umkhosi woMhlanga, the Reed Dance, is held each September at the royal palace of eNyokeni in Nongoma. Tens of thousands of young women in traditional dress carry long reeds to present to the king, celebrating womanhood and the protection of young people. Umkhosi Wokweshwama, the first fruits festival, is another royal celebration.
Music and dance

Zulu music is famous worldwide. Isicathamiya, a soft-stepping a cappella style born among Zulu migrant workers in the hostels of Durban and Johannesburg, was made famous by Ladysmith Black Mambazo, who sang with Paul Simon on the album Graceland (1986) and won several Grammy Awards. Maskandi is guitar music rooted in Zulu tradition, and indlamu is a high-kicking warrior dance. The song 'Mbube' by Solomon Linda (1939) became 'The Lion Sleeps Tonight'.
Food

Isitshwala or uphuthu, crumbly maize porridge, is eaten with amasi (thick sour milk), a much-loved combination. Other foods include izinkobe (boiled maize and beans), amadumbe (taro), chakalaka (spicy relish) and umqombothi, traditional sorghum beer brewed for ceremonies and honouring the ancestors.
Language and proverbs

isiZulu is a Bantu language with click consonants borrowed from Khoisan languages, written c, q and x. Sawubona means 'I see you' as a greeting, and the reply Yebo means 'Yes'.

• 'Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu.' A person is a person through other people (the heart of Ubuntu).
• 'Izandla ziyagezana.' Hands wash each other.
• 'Inkunzi isematholeni.' The bull is among the calves (greatness can be found in the young).
The Zulu today

The Zulu monarchy continues as a cultural institution recognised by South Africa's constitution. King Goodwill Zwelithini reigned from 1971 until his death in 2021, and his son Misuzulu kaZwelithini became king. Zulu leaders and voters have shaped national politics, and Zulu culture, music and language are central to South African life. Nelson Mandela's successor Jacob Zuma, president from 2009 to 2018, is Zulu.
Did you know?

• Shaka Zulu's name lives on in King Shaka International Airport in Durban.
• 16 December, once a Boer commemoration, is now South Africa's Day of Reconciliation.
• The Drakensberg mountains are called uKhahlamba, 'barrier of spears', in isiZulu.
Sources and further reading
