peoples.name: Xhosa
peoples.blurb: The people of Nelson Mandela, who fought a century of frontier wars, speak a language rich in clicks, and honour the journey into manhood.
sections: Overview

The Xhosa (amaXhosa) live mainly in the Eastern Cape of South Africa, between the Great Fish River and the Mthatha area, with large communities in Cape Town and other cities. isiXhosa is the second most spoken home language in South Africa.

The Xhosa are a Nguni people, closely related to the Zulu, Swazi and Ndebele. The wider Xhosa-speaking group includes the Gcaleka and Rharhabe (Xhosa proper), Thembu, Mpondo, Mpondomise, Bomvana and others.
Origins

The Xhosa trace their royal line to a king called Xhosa, many generations ago, and later to Tshawe, who founded the ruling house. In the 18th century the kingdom divided after a dispute between Phalo's sons into two branches: the Gcaleka, east of the Kei river, and the Rharhabe, to the west.

The Xhosa lived alongside Khoikhoi and San peoples for centuries and intermarried with them, which is why isiXhosa contains so many click sounds borrowed from Khoisan languages.
The Frontier Wars

From 1779 to 1879 the Xhosa fought nine wars against Dutch and then British colonists over land and cattle along the eastern frontier of the Cape Colony, the longest African resistance to colonial expansion in southern Africa. Leaders such as Ngqika, Ndlambe, Hintsa, Maqoma and Sandile defended their lands.

In 1819 the prophet Makhanda (Nxele) led a bold attack on Grahamstown; he was captured and died escaping from Robben Island. In 1835 King Hintsa was killed by British soldiers while under a promise of safe conduct, his body mutilated, an act still remembered with grief.
The cattle-killing of 1856 to 1857

After years of war, land loss and a lung disease that killed cattle, a young girl named Nongqawuse prophesied in 1856 that if the Xhosa killed their cattle and destroyed their grain, the ancestors would rise, new cattle would come and the British would be swept into the sea. Many believed, including King Sarhili. Around 400,000 cattle were killed.

When the prophecy failed, a terrible famine followed in which tens of thousands died and many survivors were forced to seek work in the colony. The Cape government used the disaster to seize more land. It remains one of the most tragic episodes in South African history.
Society and initiation

Family and clan are central to Xhosa identity. Every person belongs to a clan (isiduko), such as the Madiba, Dlamini, Tshawe or Mpondomise, and clan names are used as respectful forms of address. Reciting one's clan praises is a way of honouring ancestors.

Ulwaluko, the initiation of young men into adulthood, is one of the most important traditions. Young men (abakhwetha) are circumcised and spend weeks in a secluded lodge, their bodies covered in white clay, learning the responsibilities of manhood from elders. They return as amakrwala (new men) in new clothes, and the old lodge is burned. Girls have their own coming-of-age rite, intonjane.
Beliefs

Traditional belief honours uQamata or uThixo as the creator and the ancestors (izinyanya) as guides. Diviners, amagqirha, are called by the ancestors, often through illness and dreams, and undergo long training. Christianity spread early among the Xhosa through missions such as Lovedale, and the Xhosa clergyman Tiyo Soga translated the Bible and Pilgrim's Progress into isiXhosa in the 19th century. Enoch Sontonga, a Xhosa teacher, composed 'Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika' in 1897, now part of South Africa's national anthem.
Dress, beadwork and art

Xhosa traditional dress includes blankets and skirts dyed with ochre or decorated with black braid, elaborate beadwork collars, and turbans (iqhiya) wound in many styles by married women. White clay is applied to the face for protection and beauty. The long-stemmed pipe is a symbol of a respected elder woman. Beadwork patterns and colours indicate age, status and region.
Nelson Mandela and the struggle

Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born in 1918 in Mvezo, into the Thembu royal house, and is known by his clan name, Madiba. He became a lawyer, a leader of the African National Congress and of its armed wing, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1964, spending 27 years in prison, 18 of them on Robben Island. Released in 1990, he negotiated the end of apartheid and became South Africa's first democratically elected president in 1994, serving until 1999. He won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 with F. W. de Klerk.

Many other leaders of the struggle were Xhosa, including Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Steve Biko, Chris Hani and Thabo Mbeki, who succeeded Mandela as president.
Food

Umngqusho, samp (crushed dried maize) cooked with beans, was famously Nelson Mandela's favourite dish. Umphokoqo is crumbly maize porridge eaten with amasi (sour milk), and umqombothi is a traditional sorghum and maize beer brewed for ceremonies and to welcome guests.
Language and proverbs

isiXhosa has three main click sounds: c (dental, like a 'tsk' of disapproval), q (a popping sound from the roof of the mouth) and x (a lateral click from the side of the tongue), each with variations. The word 'Xhosa' itself begins with a click.

• 'Umntu ngumntu ngabantu.' A person is a person through other people.
• 'Akukho nkomo inqoba ilanga.' No cow can defeat the sun (no one can stop time).
• 'Isisu somzi asinambeleko.' The stomach of a homestead has no carrying blanket (family matters are private).
Did you know?

• Miriam Makeba's 'Qongqothwane', known as 'The Click Song', made Xhosa clicks famous worldwide.
• Mandela's name Rolihlahla means 'pulling the branch of a tree', or informally, 'troublemaker'.
• The fictional nation of Wakanda in the film Black Panther used isiXhosa as its language.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Shona
peoples.blurb: Builders of Great Zimbabwe, the largest stone city south of the Sahara, masters of the mbira and of world-famous stone sculpture.
peoples.population: About 13 to 15 million people, most of Zimbabwe's population
sections: Overview

The Shona are the largest group in Zimbabwe, making up the majority of the country's population, with communities in Mozambique, Botswana and South Africa. They include several major dialect groups: Zezuru, Karanga, Manyika, Korekore and Ndau.

The Shona are heirs to some of Africa's greatest civilisations, including Great Zimbabwe and the Mutapa state, and they gave their country its name: Zimbabwe comes from the Shona dzimba dza mabwe, 'houses of stone'.
Great Zimbabwe

Great Zimbabwe, near modern Masvingo, was built between about the 11th and 15th centuries by the ancestors of the Shona. At its height in the 14th century it may have had a population of around 10,000 to 18,000 people and was the capital of a powerful kingdom.

It has three main parts: the Hill Complex, a royal and religious centre built among granite boulders; the Great Enclosure, whose curving outer wall is up to 11 metres high and about 250 metres long, built of granite blocks fitted together without mortar and decorated with a chevron pattern; and the Valley ruins, where ordinary people lived. Inside the Great Enclosure stands a solid conical tower about 10 metres tall, perhaps symbolising a grain bin.

Great Zimbabwe grew rich from cattle and from the gold trade with the Swahili coast: Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and glass beads from India have been found there. It was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
The Zimbabwe Birds and the colonial myth

Eight carved soapstone birds were found at Great Zimbabwe, each on top of a tall pillar, probably representing royal ancestors or the bateleur eagle, a messenger of the spirits. The Zimbabwe Bird is now the national emblem, on the flag and the coat of arms. Several birds were taken to South Africa in the colonial era; most have been returned.

When Europeans 'discovered' Great Zimbabwe in the 1870s, many refused to believe that Africans could have built it, and attributed it to the Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba. The Rhodesian government even censored archaeologists. Research, beginning with Gertrude Caton-Thompson in 1929, proved beyond doubt that it was built by the ancestors of the Shona.
The Mutapa and Rozvi states

As Great Zimbabwe declined in the 15th century, power shifted north. Around 1430 Nyatsimba Mutota founded the Mutapa (Monomotapa) state, whose rulers bore the title Mwene Mutapa, 'lord of the conquered lands'. Mutapa controlled gold fields and trade with the Swahili and then the Portuguese, who tried and failed to conquer it in the 16th and 17th centuries.

In the south-west, the Torwa state and later the Rozvi Empire under Changamire Dombo rose in the late 17th century, driving the Portuguese from the plateau. Stone-walled sites such as Khami and Danangombe (Dhlo-Dhlo) belong to this era.
Religion and the spirit mediums

Shona belief centres on Mwari, the high God, and on ancestral spirits. Family ancestors (vadzimu) protect their descendants, while mhondoro, the spirits of great royal ancestors, are guardians of the land, rain and fertility, speaking through spirit mediums (svikiro). The Matopos hills hold shrines of Mwari, where oracles were consulted.

At the bira ceremony, families gather through the night with mbira music, singing and beer to call the ancestors.
Mbira: the voice of the ancestors

The mbira dzavadzimu, 'mbira of the ancestors', has 22 to 28 metal keys mounted on a hardwood board, often placed inside a large calabash resonator and fitted with shells or bottle caps that buzz. Players pluck the keys with thumbs and a forefinger in interlocking patterns while singers improvise. In 2020 UNESCO recognised the art of crafting and playing mbira as Intangible Cultural Heritage. Musicians such as Thomas Mapfumo, Stella Chiweshe and Chiwoniso brought mbira-based music to the world.
Mbuya Nehanda and the First Chimurenga

When Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company occupied the country in 1890, naming it Rhodesia, it seized land and cattle. In 1896 to 1897 the Ndebele and Shona rose in the First Chimurenga (war of liberation). Spirit mediums played leading roles, especially Charwe Nyakasikana, the medium of the spirit Nehanda, and Sekuru Kaguvi.

Nehanda was captured and hanged in 1898. Tradition says she declared, 'My bones will rise again.' Seventy years later, guerrillas of the Second Chimurenga saw themselves as the fulfilment of that prophecy. A statue of Mbuya Nehanda was unveiled in Harare in 2021.
Independence and today

After white-minority Rhodesia declared independence unilaterally in 1965, nationalist movements fought a liberation war through the 1970s. Zimbabwe became independent on 18 April 1980.

Shona stone sculpture, carved from serpentine and springstone by artists such as Nicholas Mukomberanwa, Henry Munyaradzi and Dominic Benhura, became internationally celebrated from the 1960s and is exhibited in major museums. Tengenenge in northern Zimbabwe is a famous artists' community.
Food

Sadza, a stiff porridge of maize meal (or millet and sorghum in the past), is the daily staple, eaten with relish (usavi) such as covo greens, beef stew, dried kapenta fish, mushrooms or nyimo beans. Maputi is popped maize, and mazhanje (wild loquats) are a favourite seasonal fruit. Mahewu is a fermented maize drink.
Language and proverbs

Shona is a Bantu language, tonal, with the famous 'whistled' sounds sv and zv. Totems (mutupo), such as shumba (lion), soko (monkey), nzou (elephant) and moyo (heart), link families to clans and are used in respectful greetings and praise poetry.

• 'Chara chimwe hachitswanyi inda.' One thumb cannot crush a louse (cooperation is needed).
• 'Kure kwegava ndokusina mutsubvu.' The jackal's far place is where there is no fruit tree (people travel far for what they need).
• 'Rina manyanga hariputirwe.' What has horns cannot be wrapped (the truth comes out).
Did you know?

• The walls of Great Zimbabwe's Great Enclosure contain about 900,000 stone blocks.
• The bateleur eagle, believed to carry messages to the ancestors, is one candidate for the bird on Zimbabwe's flag.
• Victoria Falls is known in the Lozi and Tonga languages as Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'.

peoples.name: Oromo
peoples.blurb: Ethiopia's largest people, keepers of the Gadaa democratic system and of the Irreecha thanksgiving festival.
peoples.population: About 40 million people, the largest ethnic group in Ethiopia
sections: Overview

The Oromo are the largest ethnic group in Ethiopia, making up around a third of the population, and also live in northern Kenya. Their homeland, Oromia, stretches across the centre, west and south of Ethiopia, including the area around the capital Addis Ababa (Finfinne in Afaan Oromoo).

Afaan Oromoo is one of the most widely spoken languages in Africa. The Oromo include many branches, such as the Tulama, Macha, Arsi, Borana, Guji, Karrayyu and Wallo, with diverse ways of life: highland farmers, lowland pastoralists, traders and city dwellers.
Origins and the great expansion

The Oromo are a Cushitic people whose ancestors lived in the highlands and lowlands of southern Ethiopia for a very long time. In the 16th century they began a remarkable expansion northward and westward, often called the Oromo migrations, reaching the central highlands, Wallo, the Gibe region and Harar. This movement was organised through the Gadaa system, with each new Gadaa class leading campaigns.

In the 18th and 19th centuries several Oromo monarchies emerged in the Gibe region, such as Jimma, Limmu-Ennarea, Gera and Gumma, rich in coffee, gold and ivory trade. Jimma under Abba Jifar II (reigned 1878 to 1932) was famous for its prosperity and its palace.
The Gadaa system

Gadaa is a traditional system of government, law and social organisation. Men are grouped into classes (luba) that pass through a series of grades every eight years, each grade with its own duties: childhood, learning, warrior training, and then holding political power. The class in power elects leaders, including the Abbaa Gadaa (father of Gadaa), who serve for one eight-year term only, after which power passes peacefully to the next class.

Laws are made and reviewed at a general assembly, the Gumii Gaayoo among the Borana, held under sacred trees. Leaders can be removed if they fail. Women had a parallel institution, Siiqqee, a symbolic stick representing women's rights and their power to protest injustice.

UNESCO inscribed the Gadaa system on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2016, recognising it as an indigenous democratic socio-political system.
Religion: Waaqeffannaa and Irreecha

The traditional Oromo religion, Waaqeffannaa, worships Waaqa, the one sky God, creator of all things. Qaalluu, ritual leaders, guided the community, and sacred places included mountains, rivers, lakes and the odaa, the great sycamore fig tree under which assemblies met; the odaa is a symbol of the Oromo people.

Irreecha is a thanksgiving festival held at the end of the rainy season, around late September or early October, when millions of people gather at Lake Hora Arsadi in Bishoftu, and in spring at Mount Furi near Addis Ababa, carrying fresh green grass and flowers to the water to thank Waaqa for the passing of the rains and to pray for peace and plenty.

Today most Oromo are Muslim or Christian (Orthodox and Protestant), but Irreecha remains a powerful cultural celebration for all.
Under the Ethiopian Empire

In the late 19th century Emperor Menelik II conquered most Oromo lands and incorporated them into the Ethiopian Empire. Land was given to northern settlers and officials, and many Oromo became tenants on their own land. Afaan Oromoo was discouraged in schools and public life for much of the 20th century, and Amharic was promoted as the national language.

Oromo resistance and cultural movements grew, including the Macha-Tulama Self-Help Association in the 1960s. After 1991 Ethiopia adopted a federal system, and Oromia became a regional state with Afaan Oromoo as its official language. In 2018 Abiy Ahmed, of Oromo and Amhara heritage, became prime minister, and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for making peace with Eritrea.
Society and family

Oromo society values age, respect for elders and collective decisions. Clans and lineages are important, and the naming of children, marriage and conflict resolution follow customary law (seera). Elders, jaarsa biyyaa, mediate disputes through traditional reconciliation called jaarsummaa. Cattle are wealth among pastoral groups such as the Borana, and the singing wells of Borana, where men pass water hand to hand while singing, are famous.
Coffee and food

Coffee grows wild in the forests of south-western Ethiopia, and Oromo areas such as Jimma, Limmu, Sidama's neighbours and Harar are famous for it. Buna qalaa is a ritual dish of coffee beans roasted in butter, shared to bless important events.

Oromo foods include injera with wat (stews), marqaa (porridge), chuko (roasted barley with butter and spices), and ittoo (vegetable stew). Milk and butter are central among pastoral Oromo.
Runners

Many of Ethiopia's legendary distance runners are Oromo, including Abebe Bikila, who won the Olympic marathon in Rome in 1960 running barefoot, the first Olympic gold for a Black African; Haile Gebrselassie, Kenenisa Bekele, Derartu Tulu (the first Black African woman to win Olympic gold, in 1992) and Tirunesh Dibaba. The highlands of Arsi around Bekoji are known as a 'town of runners'.
Language and proverbs

Afaan Oromoo is a Cushitic language of the Afroasiatic family, related to Somali and Afar. Since 1991 it has been written with the Latin-based Qubee alphabet.

• 'Harka fudhatanii, harka kennu.' One receives with the hand and gives with the hand.
• 'Kan dhaga'ee hin dhagahin, dhagaan dhaga'a.' What the ear has not heard, a stone hears (secrets come out).
• 'Abbaan baay'ee, ilmaan hin gaddu.' Where there are many fathers, the children do not grieve.
Did you know?

• The legend of coffee's discovery tells of a goatherd named Kaldi whose goats danced after eating coffee berries in the Ethiopian highlands.
• An Oromo saying holds that 'a nation without Gadaa is like a body without a spine'.
• Irreecha is now one of the largest annual gatherings in Africa.
Sources and further reading

UNESCO Intangible Heritage: Gada system, an indigenous democratic socio-political system of the Oromo (2016); Asmarom Legesse, Oromo Democracy; Mohammed Hassen, The Oromo of Ethiopia: A History 1570 to 1860; Wikipedia: Oromo people, Gadaa, Irreecha.

peoples.name: Amhara
peoples.blurb: Heirs of the Solomonic emperors and the rock churches of Lalibela, whose language, Amharic, is written in the ancient Ge'ez script.
sections: Overview

The Amhara live in the highlands of northern and central Ethiopia, in the Amhara region around Lake Tana, Gondar, Bahir Dar, Dessie and Debre Birhan, and throughout the country. They are the second largest ethnic group in Ethiopia.

Amharic, their language, has been the working language of the Ethiopian state for centuries and is spoken as a second language by tens of millions. The Amhara are closely linked with the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the history of the Ethiopian monarchy.
Aksum and the Solomonic tradition

The roots of Amhara civilisation go back to the Kingdom of Aksum (about 1st to 7th centuries CE), one of the great powers of the ancient world, which minted its own coins and adopted Christianity under King Ezana in the 4th century, one of the first states in the world to do so.

The Kebra Nagast, 'Glory of the Kings', a 14th-century book, tells that the Queen of Sheba (Makeda) visited King Solomon in Jerusalem and bore him a son, Menelik I, who brought the Ark of the Covenant to Aksum. The Solomonic dynasty, which claimed descent from Menelik, came to power in 1270 under Yekuno Amlak and ruled, with interruptions, until 1974.
Lalibela and the Zagwe

Between Aksum and the Solomonic restoration, the Zagwe dynasty ruled. Its most famous king, Lalibela (late 12th to early 13th century), ordered the carving of eleven churches directly out of solid volcanic rock in the town that now bears his name, intended as a 'New Jerusalem'. Bete Giyorgis (the Church of St George), cut in the shape of a cross deep into the ground, is one of the wonders of world architecture. The Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978, among the first ever listed.
Gondar and the Era of the Princes

In 1636 Emperor Fasilides founded Gondar as a permanent capital, and he and his successors built castles, palaces, churches and the bathing pool of Fasil, mixing Ethiopian, Arab, Indian and European influences. The Fasil Ghebbi royal enclosure is a UNESCO site.

From 1769 to 1855, during the Zemene Mesafint (Era of the Princes), emperors were figureheads while regional lords fought for power. Tewodros II reunified the empire in 1855 and began modernisation, but died at Magdala in 1868 during a British expedition.
Adwa and independence

Emperor Menelik II, of Shewan Amhara descent, expanded Ethiopia to roughly its modern borders and founded Addis Ababa in 1886. When Italy tried to make Ethiopia a protectorate, Menelik and Empress Taytu gathered an army from across the empire. On 1 March 1896, at the Battle of Adwa, Ethiopian forces decisively defeated the Italian army, killing thousands and capturing many prisoners.

Adwa made Ethiopia a symbol of African freedom: it was the only African nation (alongside Liberia) to remain independent during the Scramble for Africa. Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941 under Mussolini, but Emperor Haile Selassie returned after British and Ethiopian forces defeated the Italians. Haile Selassie helped found the Organisation of African Unity in Addis Ababa in 1963. He was overthrown in 1974 by the Derg military junta, which ruled until 1991.
Religion

Most Amhara belong to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, one of the oldest Christian churches in the world. Every church holds a tabot, a replica of the Ark of the Covenant, carried in procession at festivals. The church has its own calendar, with 13 months, and its own liturgical language, Ge'ez.

Timkat (Epiphany, around 19 January) celebrates the baptism of Christ with colourful processions to water, and Meskel (late September) celebrates the finding of the True Cross with huge bonfires. Both are UNESCO-listed. There are also Amhara Muslims, especially in Wallo.
Script and literature

Amharic is written in the Ge'ez script, called fidel, an abugida in which each character represents a consonant-vowel combination; there are over 200 characters. Ge'ez writing goes back to Aksumite inscriptions over 1,500 years old. Ethiopian monasteries preserve ancient illuminated manuscripts, including the Garima Gospels, among the oldest illustrated Christian manuscripts in the world.

Amharic poetry is famous for 'wax and gold' (sem-ena-werq), verses with a surface meaning (the wax) hiding a deeper one (the gold).
Food and the coffee ceremony

Injera, a large spongy flatbread made from fermented teff flour, is the heart of every meal, served with wat (spicy stews) such as doro wat (chicken), misir wat (lentils) and shiro (chickpea), seasoned with berbere spice and niter kibbeh (spiced butter). Eating together from one platter and feeding each other a mouthful (gursha) is a sign of love.

The coffee ceremony, buna, is central to social life: beans are roasted over charcoal, ground, and brewed three times in a clay jebena, with incense burning. The three rounds, abol, tona and bereka, bring blessings.
Language and proverbs

Amharic is a Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family, related to Tigrinya, Arabic and Hebrew. It is the second most spoken Semitic language in the world after Arabic.

• 'Kas be kas enkulal be egru yihedal.' Little by little, an egg will walk on its own legs.
• 'Dir biyabir anbessa yasir.' When spider webs unite, they can tie up a lion.
• 'Yalateyem lij yalamalig yitallem.' The child who is not taught at home will be taught by the world.
Did you know?

• Ethiopia uses its own calendar, about seven to eight years behind the Gregorian one, and celebrates New Year (Enkutatash) in September.
• Lucy (Dinkinesh, 'you are marvellous' in Amharic), a 3.2-million-year-old human ancestor, was found in Ethiopia's Afar region in 1974.
• Bob Marley and the Rastafari movement revere Emperor Haile Selassie.
Sources and further reading

peoples.name: Somali
peoples.region: Somalia, Djibouti, eastern Ethiopia and north-eastern Kenya
peoples.blurb: A nation of poets and camel herders on the Horn of Africa, heirs of the ancient Land of Punt and of great trading sultanates.
sections: Overview

The Somali people live across the Horn of Africa: in Somalia, Djibouti, the Somali Region of Ethiopia and north-eastern Kenya, with a large diaspora in the Middle East, Europe and North America. They share a common language, Somali, a common faith, Islam, and a strong clan-based social structure.

Traditionally many Somalis were nomadic pastoralists herding camels, goats and sheep across dry lands, while others farmed along the Juba and Shabelle rivers or traded in coastal cities such as Mogadishu, Berbera, Zeila and Barawa.
Ancient times: Punt and frankincense

The Horn of Africa has been inhabited for a very long time. The cave paintings of Laas Geel, near Hargeisa, about 5,000 years old, show cattle with ceremonial robes and people raising their arms, among the best preserved rock art in Africa.

Many historians believe the Land of Punt, the 'Land of the Gods' visited by Egyptian expeditions such as that of Queen Hatshepsut around 1470 BCE, lay on the coasts of the Horn, possibly including parts of today's Somali lands. Punt supplied Egypt with frankincense, myrrh, ebony, gold and exotic animals. Somali lands still produce some of the world's finest frankincense and myrrh. Greek and Roman sailors' guides, such as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE), describe trading ports along this coast.
Islam and the sultanates

Islam reached the Somali coast very early, within the first century of the faith, through trade across the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden; the Masjid al-Qiblatayn in Zeila is said to be one of the oldest mosques in Africa. Coastal cities became prosperous Islamic centres.

The Sultanate of Mogadishu flourished from the 12th century; the traveller Ibn Battuta visited in 1331 and described its wealthy merchants and fine cloth exported to Egypt. The Ajuran Sultanate controlled much of southern Somalia from the 13th to 17th centuries, building water wells and fortifications. In the north-west, the Sultanate of Adal, based at Zeila and later Harar, became powerful; in the 16th century its imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi (Ahmad Gurey) conquered much of Ethiopia before being killed in 1543. Later states included the Geledi Sultanate and the Majeerteen and Hobyo Sultanates.
Clans and customary law

Somali society is organised around clans traced through the male line. The major clan families include the Darod, Hawiye, Dir, Isaaq and the Digil and Mirifle (Rahanweyn). A person can recite their lineage back many generations, which defines rights, obligations and alliances.

Customary law, xeer, governs relations between clans: it sets compensation (mag, or diya) for injuries and deaths, protects travellers and guests, and is administered by elders who meet under a tree to settle disputes. Xeer existed long before modern states and still plays a major role.
Camels and nomadic life

Somali lands have one of the largest camel populations in the world. The camel is the most valued animal: it provides milk, meat and transport, is used in bride wealth and compensation, and is celebrated in hundreds of poems. A man's wealth was counted in camels.

Nomadic families live in portable huts (aqal) made of curved poles covered with woven mats and hides, which women build and take down when the family moves to new pastures with the rains.
A nation of poets

Somalis are famous as a 'nation of poets'. Poetry is the most respected art form and has been used for centuries to praise, mock, negotiate peace, declare war and record history. Classical forms include the gabay (long, serious poems), geeraar (war and horse poems) and buraambur (poetry by women).

The great poet Sayyid Mohammed Abdullah Hassan led the Dervish State from 1899 to 1920 in resistance to British, Italian and Ethiopian forces, and used poetry as a weapon; the British finally defeated the Dervishes with aircraft in 1920. Twentieth-century poets such as Hadraawi and Gaarriye are household names, and modern Somali music grew from the qaraami love songs of Hargeisa.
Colonial era and independence

In the late 19th century Somali lands were divided between Britain (British Somaliland), Italy (Italian Somaliland), France (French Somaliland, now Djibouti), Ethiopia (the Ogaden) and Britain's Kenya Colony. On 1 July 1960 British Somaliland and Italian Somaliland united to form the Somali Republic. The five-pointed star on Somalia's flag represents the five regions where Somalis live.

After 1991 the central state collapsed and Somalia endured civil war; Somaliland in the north-west declared independence, which has not been internationally recognised. Despite great hardship, Somalis rebuilt businesses, telecommunications and money-transfer systems, and the diaspora contributes hugely.
Writing the language

For centuries Somali was spoken but rarely written, though Arabic script (Wadaad's writing) and the Osmanya script, invented by Osman Yusuf Kenadid in the 1920s, were used. In 1972 the government adopted a Latin-based alphabet, and a massive literacy campaign followed. Somali is a Cushitic language of the Afroasiatic family, related to Oromo and Afar.
Food

Somali cuisine blends African, Arabian, Indian and Italian influences. Favourites include bariis iskukaris (spiced rice with meat), suqaar (small pieces of sautéed meat), canjeero or lahoh (a spongy pancake eaten at breakfast), sambuusa, and halwo, a sweet, sticky dessert served at weddings and Eid. Camel milk and camel meat are prized, and spaghetti (baasto), introduced by the Italians, is a popular dish eaten with a banana on the side.
Proverbs

• 'Aqoon la'aan waa iftiin la'aan.' Being without knowledge is being without light.
• 'Nin aan dhul marin dhaayo ma leh.' A man who has not travelled has no eyes.
• 'Gacmo wada jir bay wax ku gooyaan.' Hands cut things when working together.
Did you know?

• Somalia has the longest coastline of any country on the African mainland, over 3,000 km.
• The Somali shilling once carried images of camels, and camel racing is a popular sport.
• Iman, the supermodel, and Mo Farah, the Olympic champion, are of Somali heritage.
